doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: First loves: Henry Mancini, radio DJs and his sister's records
summary: As a child he discovers jazz through Mancini film scores, Billy Taylor's radio show, and his sister's eclectic record collection.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yes, yeah. That’s kind of a mouthful. It’s not the easiest thing to do. But one thing I learned early on, even as a teenager, was the ability to enjoy all genres of music. So jazz has always been my foundation. As a matter of fact my first real introduction to jazz was watching TV and looking at “Peter Gunn” and “Mr. Lucky,” which was scored by Henry Mancini. So needless to say Henry Mancini had an integral part in my development as a musician and a music lover. And I used to go to every film he scored. And sometimes the films were horrible. But I mean I just had to go because I absorbed his music so much. I became kind of an expert on his musical style and his way with horns and how he used it dramatically in film. And from there I started listening to him on the radio, and from there I was introduced to Billy Taylor, because he was a DJ on a local radio station. He was on NEW, a station called WNEW, then he moved to a station called LIB, which is still happening right now but it’s all R&B. They had like a whole jazz thing. So by listening to Billy and his roster of music, and the other two DJs that were on that same station, I got introduced to Dizzy and Gil Evans and Miles. This was like in the ‘60s, all these wonderful musicians. And I used to make a list — now mind you I’m all of like nine, ten, eleven years old — and I’m making a list of all these songs I heard on the radio that I liked. Like I’ve got to get that one, I’ve got to get that one. And my sister also had an impact on me because she had a very eclectic taste as a teenager. I mean most teenagers now would have one style of music in their repertoire. And at this time, like at sixteen years old, she had Barbra Streisand, Johnny Mathis, Igor Stravinsky, Sonny Rollins, Loretta Alexandria, Johnny Pacheco, you know it was just endless, of all these different — Nat King Cole, Nina Simone.
